title: ReNU SYNDROME
alt_titles: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, BRAIN ANOMALIES, DISTINCTIVE FACIES, AND ABSENT LANGUAGE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene on chromosome 12. Most of these mutations occur de novo.

checks.claim: ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We implicated de novo variants among 47 cases in two regions of RNU4-2 in the etiology of a syndrome characterized by ID, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures and motor delay.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a dominant association and heterozygous calls. 'ReNU syndrome' is the later name for this syndrome.

checks.claim: The RNU4-2 gene is located on chromosome 12.
checks.evidence_quote: RNU4-2, which encodes U4 small nuclear RNA, a critical component of the spliceosome, was the most strongly associated gene.
checks.explanation: The paper does not give the chromosome. A gene's chromosomal location counts as standard nomenclature under the rules.

checks.claim: Most RNU4-2 mutations causing ReNU syndrome occur de novo.
checks.evidence_quote: Of the 47 rare allele instances in the regions, which we observed in 47 cases, 37 were determined to be de novo

paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by moderate to severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and absent or very limited speech. Other common features are hypotonia, microcephaly, short stature, seizures, and brain MRI abnormalities. Many patients also have distinctive facial features and problems in several organ systems, including the eyes, gastrointestinal tract, and skeleton. The disorder is caused by heterozygous, mostly de novo, mutations in a short critical region of RNU4-2, the gene encoding the U4 small nuclear RNA of the major spliceosome (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) reviewed Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms for 46 cases from the 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP) who carried RNU4-2 variants and had a neurodevelopmental abnormality. Of these, 91% had intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay. Several terms were significantly more frequent than in other cases with a neurodevelopmental abnormality: microcephaly (57%), drooling (13%), proportionate short stature (28%), generalized hypotonia (39%), seizures (52%), and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion (13%).

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed clinical information on 49 individuals (21 females and 28 males; median age at last evaluation, 10 years; range, 2 to 38 years) with RNU4-2 variants. All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Of those older than 5 years, 83% could walk, although walking was delayed (average age 3.4 years; range, 17 months to 7.5 years). Some had a wide-based or ataxic gait. Most patients were nonverbal, some had a few words, and only 3 had fluent speech. Short stature was present in 76% and microcephaly in 77%; the microcephaly was mostly congenital. Other features included hypotonia (87%), seizures (77%), behavioral problems (67%), autism spectrum disorder (48%), sleep problems (47%), and intrauterine growth restriction (18%). Seizure onset varied, with a median of 3 years and a range from the first year of life to 10 years. Seizure types included infantile spasms, focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizures, and status epilepticus. Brain MRI was abnormal in 91%. The most frequent findings were reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination.

paragraphs.text: In the same cohort, Chen et al. (2024) found dysmorphic facial features in 94% of patients. These included a myopathic face, deep-set eyes (widely or narrowly spaced), epicanthus, a wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, and large cupped ears, some posteriorly rotated. Other facial features were full cheeks, full lips with downturned corners, a high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. Visual problems were reported in 79%, including strabismus (51%), nystagmus (45%), optic nerve hypoplasia (22%), and cortical blindness. Hearing loss occurred in 22%. Gastrointestinal problems included feeding difficulties (76%), constipation (66%), and gastroesophageal reflux (49%); 32% needed a gastrostomy tube. Skeletal findings (64%) included osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and hip dysplasia. Endocrine problems (44%) included hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, and pituitary abnormalities. Limb, genitourinary, dental, cardiac, and skin problems were also reported. Presentation did not differ significantly between males and females.

paragraphs.text: Heterozygous RNU4-2 mutations in ReNU syndrome usually occur de novo (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Greene et al. (2024) described 1 case in which the patient inherited the n.76C-T variant from an affected mother. They also found that the mother of a patient with n.65A-G was mosaic for the variant. Chen et al. (2024) determined the parent of origin in 54 individuals and found the variant on the maternal allele in all of them.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) performed a rare-variant association analysis of 41,132 noncoding genes using whole-genome sequencing data from the 100KGP. They compared 5,529 unrelated cases with intellectual disability against 46,401 unrelated controls. RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 small nuclear RNA (snRNA), showed the strongest association by far (posterior probability of association approximately 1). Variants were found in 47 cases and fell in 2 regions, nucleotides n.62-70 and n.73-79, where no unaffected participants carried rare variants. These regions map to the U4-U6 quasi-pseudoknot and to stem III. Of the 47 variants, 37 were de novo and 10 had unknown inheritance. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, arose de novo in 33 families. In replication cohorts (the NIHR BioResource, the 100KGP Pilot, and the Genomic Medicine Service), the authors found 26 more affected probands. In 19 of them the variant was de novo. In the 100KGP, RNU4-2 accounted for 0.50% of cases with a neurodevelopmental abnormality, more than any other gene. In the Genomic Medicine Service it accounted for 0.38%, second only to MECP2. The authors suggested that disruption of the U4-U6 interaction might delay U4-U6 unwinding.

paragraphs.text: Schot et al. (2024) reanalyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 164 trios with neurodevelopmental or multiple congenital anomaly disorders. paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) found heterozygous variants in an 18-bp critical region of RNU4-2 (nucleotides 62-79) in 115 individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders, drawn from Genomics England and other cohorts. This region is strongly depleted of variation in population datasets. Of the 115 individuals, 89 (77.4%) had the recurrent n.64_65insT variant. Sequencing data from both parents in 86 individuals confirmed de novo occurrence. Single-base insertions in the region were strongly enriched in patients: 54 of 8,841 undiagnosed probands with neurodevelopmental disorders carried one, compared with 2 of 490,132 UK Biobank individuals. SNVs were only modestly enriched. Chen et al. (2024) performed RNA sequencing of blood from 5 patients. Compared with controls, patients used unannotated 5-prime splice sites more often, and these sites deviated from consensus at the +3, +4, and +5 positions, which pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence. RNU4-2 was expressed in the developing brain at much higher levels than RNU4-1. The authors estimated that variants in the critical region explain about 0.4% of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) found the heterozygous n.64_65insT variant in 89 of 115 individuals (77.4%) with neurodevelopmental disorders and variants in the RNU4-2 critical region. In Genomics England it had arisen de novo in 38 probands with unaffected parents. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant in 8 individuals. It was absent from 76,215 genomes in gnomAD v4.0 and from 245,400 individuals in the All of Us dataset, and it was seen once in the UK Biobank. In all 46 patients in whom parental origin could be determined, the variant was on the maternal allele. RNA sequencing of blood from patients with this and other RNU4-2 variants showed increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites.
